The '''Nuristani Etymological Dictionary (NurED)''' is an online etymological dictionary of the Nuristani languages, a group of Indo-Iranian languages spoken in eastern Afghanistan and northern Pakistan. The dictionary is continually updated.

It contains the results of the project ""An Etymological Dictionary of the Nuristani Nominal Lexicon"" (2023-2025) funded by the German Research Foundation within the Walter Benjamin Program (project no. 526002798). Additional entries will be continually added in the course of the project ""The Linguistic (Pre-)History of the Indo-Iranian Frontier"", funded by the German Research Foundation within the Emmy Noether Program (project no. 566371522). For explanations on the structure of entries and the adopted conventions for transcription, entry lemmas, etc., see the [[Help:Guide
The easiest way to find entries is by browsing the [[#Indexes
column2: indexes]], which are organized by language/variety. Just click on the word you are interested in and you will be forwarded to the entry or entries where it is mentioned. Alternatively, words in any language that are mentioned in any entry can also be found via the search box on top of this page.

• Katë w kt kl ačé, obl. ačér̆-e; ne, se ačẽ́ n. m. 'woolen thread'
    [S-kt; G XI-1 (⟨acere⟩, recte ⟨ačeře⟩ 'пряжа'); SA16; SA22 ('د وړیو تار', 'نخ، تار بافت، هون'); S-km]

    [ARS]

• Yaghnobi íčin n. 'string, thread'

The Nuristani words are likely inherited since there is a genuine cognate in Pr. and external parallels exist only in Iranian languages that were not in contact with Nuristani in earlier history. Length on the first vowel can only be reconstructed based on external comparison.

See further Halfmann (2025: 109): ""Cheung (2007: 29) connects the Iranian cognates to the root of NP ā-ǰī-dan 'to sew' and OIA cī́-ra 'cloth, strip, bark' (cf. s.v. MIA *cīra) which he reconstructs as *čaiH-, but he does not give a specific reconstruction for the 'thread, yarn' words. They could be reconciled under a (pseudo-)reconstruction *ā-čiH-ana-.[1] Bailey's (1979: 1, 16) proposal *ā-čyana- is not possible because *či̯ yields ts in Khot.. Psht. inċə́y is probably also < *ā-čiH-ana-kī- and not, with NEVP (9), < *ham-č(a)yakī. Metathesis *čn > *nč is more likely, since in original *mč/*nč we would expect post-nasal voicing > nj̈ (cf. Skjærvø 1989: 403).""

• ↑ Debrunner (AiGr II, 2: 197–198) notes that -(a)na- derivatives with zero grade in the root appear in OIA especially next to class 6 presents, e.g. dhúvana- 'shaking' next to dhuvati 'shakes'. This would allow the hypothesis that the PIIr. present stem of *čaiH- may have been *čiH-a-. Perhaps the derivation is then best imagined as *čiH-a-ti > *čiyati → *čiya-na-.

Proto-Nuristani Reconstruction

• Katë w kl, kt ac̣yú; w kl, ne ac̣í; se ac̣ǘ n. f. 'tear'
    [G-gloss; G-Rec; S-kt; SA16; SA22 ('اوښکه', 'اشک'); S-km; Ġ-Q (s.v. اوښکه)]
• early attestation - Davidson 1902 (1898): se ⟨achu⟩

• Ashkun s istrū́ n. m. 'tear'
    [M-A2; M-Gl; B-w; S-s]

• Prasun ◊ üčǖ́ n. 'tear'
    [BD; M-Pr]

• Khotanese āṣka- n. 'tears'
    [DKS]

• New Persian ars, ašk n. 'tear'
    [JA]

• Pashto óx̌a n. f. 'tear'
    [ARS]

• Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱru-
    [EWA I: 138-139]
The Kt., A. and Pr. forms are identified as inherited words by the development PIIr. *ćr > PNur. *ċr > Kt. c̣, Pr. č, A. str.

Pace Turner (CDIAL: 919), A. str does not result from metathesis tsr > str. The -t- is more likely an intrusive occlusion between s (< *ċ) and r. IA cognates could independently develop the same kind of occlusion (a typologically common sound change), so that Turner's (CDIAL: 919) sociolinguistically implausible assumption that such forms in IA are borrowed from A. is not required.
NKal. üṣǘk tear, on the other hand, is more likely an IA loanword due to the development PIIr. *ćr > śr > ṣ (see s.v. MIA *aṣṣu).

Nuristani agrees with Indo-Iranian in general in showing a reflex of PIE *h₂eḱru-. Agn. (Toch. A) ākär and Lith. ãšara could also be derived from such a PIE reconstruction, but other IE branches have apparent cognates with different onsets (e.g. Hitt. išḫaḫru, Gr. δάκρυ).

Borrowing from the more easterly literary dialect in MIA times seems possible, though this particular word is not attested in a conclusive spelling. The final -k in NKal. points to additional (diminutive) suffixation.

The reconstruction *''kaṭṭi-°'' presupposed by the attested forms is not directly derivable from {{OIA}} ''kr̥ti-°'', from which we would expect something like **''kiḍi-°''. Instead they more likely reflect a ''vr̥ddhi'' form *''kārtikara-'' 'belonging/relating to a sorcerer/magician' derived from ''kr̥ti-kara-''. column1: Some of these forms have previously been connected to {{PIIr.}} *''u̯artakā-'' 'quail' (~ {{OIA}} ''vártikā-'', ''vartakā-'', {{Kho.}} ''bahrtí ~ bahtí'' [{{BKhoL}}]; {{Khot.}} ''baḍye'' [{{DKS}}], {{Oss.}} {{ir}} ''wærcc'', {{dg}} ''wærccæ'' 'quail' [{{IĖSOJa}}] etc.), but this is phonologically problematic.

Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1934}}: 82, {{Morgenstierne1973c}}: 108) therefore proposed to connect all Nuristani forms as one cognate set with {{NIA}} forms like {{IAKal.}} ''uprạhụ̃́yak'', {{u}} ''hūpra'' [{{TC}}, {{IIFL IV}}], {{Pal.}} ''ubru'' [{{M-Pal}}], {{GB}} ''umla'' 'partridge' [{{FLI-GB}}], {{Dam.}} ''umbrā'' 'quail' [{{FLI-D}}]. To this group he also associates {{NP}} ''hūbara'' 'bustard', but this appears to be of Arabic origin and therefore almost certainly unrelated.<ref>Schapka ({{Schapka1972}}: 74, 285-286): ""Im Namen ''ḥubārā'' liegt eine mit der Femininendung ''-ā'' erweiterte ''qutāl''-Bildung vor (über ''-ā-''Feminina s. W. Wright, Arabic Grammar I p. 151 §252), die in Pflanzen- und Tiernamen häufig begegnet. Von derselben Wurzel ''ḥbr'' kennen wir aus dem Arabischen einen weiteren Namen der Trappe, bes. 'Trappenjunges', ''yaḥbūr''."" ""In ''hūbara'' und ''āhū'ba(r)ra'' vermuten wir volksetymologische Umdeutung des arabischen ''ḥubārā'' im Sinne von nicht recht einleuchtendem 'Gazellen-Lamm'""</ref>

If the {{IA}} and Nuristani forms are cognate, this would make it likely that the Nuristani forms are borrowed from {{IA}}. The ultimate etymology remains, however, elusive and a reconstruction of the source word that would explain all attested forms is difficult to produce. E.g., the ''ṛ'' in the {{A.}} {{tt}} form probably cannot be derived from an earlier simple *''r'', which would make it incompatible with the {{IA}} set.

column4: rifle, blowgun}}<ref>The word is Persian in origin, not Turkic as is sometimes assumed. The current {{NP}} word for 'rifle' has the form ''tufang'', having been altered by assimilation to ''fišang'' 'cartridge' and leaving the older form ''tufak'' with only the meaning 'blowgun', but it seems to have entered into Pashto and thence into Nuristani before this alteration took place. The opposite contamination has happened in Turkish, where the outcomes are ''fişek'' 'cartridge' and ''tüfek'' 'gun'. The word ''fišang'' is borrowed from {{Gr.}} ''φυσίγγιο'' 'cartridge'. (Thiesen {{Thiesen2005}}: 213)</ref>

column5: {{B-w}} (⟨tupák ~ tüpák⟩)<ref>Variance in notation ⟨u ~ ü⟩ in Buddruss's data is due to phonetic value [ʉ] of {{A.}} /u/.</ref>, {{S-s}}, {{M-A2}}}}

column1: The source of the borrowing is evidently not the variant ''ṭupák'' with an unexplained retroflex initial, which also exists in {{Psht.}}, but the expected form with the dental. Fussman ({{Fussman1972}}: 179-180) cites a {{Kt.}} {{ne}} form ""ṭapɛk"" with a retroflex initial from Morgenstierne's field notes, which he  considers the only certain loanword from {{Psht.}} among the Nuristani 'rifle' words for this reason. However, the retroflex is most likely a notation error, as this word only appears with a dental initial today. The form with a dental is also cited by Fussman ({{Fussman1972}}) as a variant. Fussman ({{Fussman1972}}: 180) is right to point out that, though the source language of the borrowing cannot be determined as either Persian or Pashto on phonological grounds, Pashto is the more likely source for historical and geographical reasons.

The {{Kt.}} {{w}} form shows regular syncope of pre-stress ''u'', but the other two dialects have an unexpected ''a'' in the first syllable, which is reminiscent of the one that appears in ''ṣapṣí'' 'sister's child' (see {{MIA}} [[*śpaṣṣiya]]). The suffix of {{se}} ''tapkë́'' may have its origin in the phenomenon of stem-variant loanwords following the ''-ë'' declension (see Halfmann {{Halfmann2024a}}: 224-225). Oblique case suffixes from the ''-ë'' declension could have allowed the analogical restoration of a direct case form with final ''-ë́''.
An interesting hybrid form is attested in {{Kt.}} {{w}} ''tpaŋčá'' 'pistol' ({{G
column3: 21}}), which has the stem of ''tpëk'', but the suffix of {{NP}} ''tufangča'' 'pistol'.

column1: Tāza ({{Tāza2017}}: 814) notes that a common word for 'rifle' in pre-Islamic times was ''čakmák'', probably a clipping of {{Psht.}} ''čaqmaqī́ tupák'' 'flintlock rifle' (< {{Chagh.}} ''čaqmaq'' 'flint'). Firearms began to be used in Nuristan in the 19th century.

column1: Following Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1949}}: 279), these Nuristani forms have generally been held to be cognates of {{OIA}} ''vrīhi-'' 'rice', deriving from a presumable {{PIIr.}} form **''u̯rīj́<sup>h</sup>i-''. This etymology is accepted, e.g., by Turner ({{CDIAL}}: T. 12233) and Kümmel ({{Kümmel2017}}: 281, 283). However, it fails both formally, as {{PIIr.}} *''u̯r-'' produces {{Kt.}} ''br̆-'' (cf. ''br̆e'' 'flour' < [[*wre(w)i(ta)-
column3: *wriċ-]]),<ref>The variant **''wr̆iċ'' cited by Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1949}}: 279) is not confirmed anywhere and seems to be a notation error. If it existed, it would still be phonologically incompatible with {{PIIr.}} *''u̯r-''.</ref> and semantically, as rice and barley have little in common either in terms of physical attributes or of cultivation techniques. Speakers of ancestral Nuristani varieties are also unlikely to have had knowledge of rice agriculture and its terminology, which was probably borrowed into already diversified Indo-Iranian languages after its arrival in South Asia.

column1: On the other hand, the Khotanese, Tumshuqese and Khwarezmian terms mentioned above produce a plausible formal and semantic match. Kümmel ({{Kümmel2017}}: 281; against Bailey {{Bailey1979}}: 367, {{NEVP}}: 10) is probably justified in separating these Middle Iranian words from various New Iranian terms that seem to derive from something like *''arpućya-'' or *''arpaćya-'' (e.g. {{Psht.}} ''orbə́ša'' (''f.''), {{Sangl.}} ''vərvə́s'' 'barley', {{Mnj.}} ''āršíya'' 'type of barley (from central Nuristan)' [{{NEVP}}: 10, {{G-Mnj}}]).

The correspondence {{Kt.}} ''ċ'' ~ {{Pr.}} ''z'' can theoretically derive from a {{PNur.}} *''j̈'' in secondary word-final position, as required for the 'rice' etymology, but its source may just as well be a {{PNur.}} *''ċ'' < {{PIIr.}} *''ć'' (whence also {{Khot.}} and {{Khwar.}} ''s''). Some difficulties remain with regard to the vowel development. Following Morgenstierne (1949: 279), these Nuristani forms have generally been held to be cognates of OIA vrīhi- 'rice', deriving from a presumable PIIr. form **u̯rīj́hi-. This etymology is accepted, e.g., by Turner (CDIAL: T. 12233) and Kümmel (2017: 281, 283). Speakers of ancestral Nuristani varieties are also unlikely to have had knowledge of rice agriculture and its terminology, which was probably borrowed into already diversified Indo-Iranian languages after its arrival in South Asia.

column1: Terms for 'musk deer' and 'hare' appear to be colexified across the entire Hindu Kush/Karakorum region. Often only one of the two meanings is recorded in a given documentary source, but then the other appears in another source on the same language. This phenomenon was already noted by Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1940}}: 249), who also found it difficult to reconcile the various groups of similar words with this meaning attested in the region under one etymon.

A first group of clearly related forms meaning 'musk deer, deer, hare' is found in the Indo-Aryan languages from Khowar to Kashmiri and the isolate Burushaski. These forms all seem to derive from a prototype like **''ronz'', **''ranz'' or **''raunz''. The non-Indo-Aryan appearance of this word (''z'' appears even in languages that have no ''z'' in inherited vocabulary) and the limited habitat of the musk deer make it plausible to assume a loanword.

{{IAKal.}} ''ráus'' is mentioned by Steblin-Kamenskij ({{Steblin-Kamenskij1999}}: 305) in the context of Iranian words of a similar appearance which refer to the 'Marco Polo sheep' (e.g. {{Khot.}} ''rūś-'', {{Wakh.}} ''rɨš'', {{Sar.}} ''rus''), but these are better kept apart, since they show voiceless sibilants and a different meaning throughout and because they have a reasonably plausible etymology (< *''r̥ćya-'' ~ {{OIA}} ''ŕ̥śya-'' '(male of) a kind of antelope'). Burushaski has representatives of both groups with distinct meanings: ''róoz'' 'musk deer' vs. ''ruś'' 'Marco Polo sheep'.

It is hard to believe that the similarity between {{Kt.}} ''vr̆akús'', {{A.}} ''ẓakus'' and {{IAKal.}} ''ráus'' should be purely accidental, but there seems to be no way to explain the ''k'' in the Nuristani forms and the forms in {{Kt.}} dialects seem to have undergone additional irregular deformations. Further complications are added by {{Pr.}} ''ëwá'' 'hare', which Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1949}}: 275) links to the {{Kt.}} word. At most the two could be connected via the assumption of a compound between the etymon of {{Pr.}} ''ëwá'' and the 'musk deer' root (**''wāk-rauns''??), but since both elements are etymologically obscure this is rather doubtful.

The {{NKal.}} terms, which have also been mentioned in this connection (Morgenstierne {{Morgenstierne1949}}: 275), are probably not directly related. {{NKal.}} {{n}} ''wr̆oċ-waméŋ'' can synchronically be interpreted as a compound of ''wr̆oċ'' 'moss, lichen' and probably a diminutive of ''wamé'' 'sheep', which would accord well with the tendency of musk deer to graze on lichen. On the other hand, the first element of the {{NKal.}} {{ẓ}} form ''ẓɪ̃ey-wamék'' bears no resemblance to the word for 'lichen' in that dialect (''ẓawóċ''). It is doubtful whether the first elements of the two dialectal forms are cognate and, if so, whether the correspondence ''wr̆oċ'' ~ ''ẓɪ̃ey'' allows any connection with the Indo-Aryan 'musk deer' words.

The last group is formed by {{Psht.}} and some {{IA}} forms, all in languages that are in contact with {{Psht.}}. In terms of biogeography it is more likely that the {{Psht.}} word is ultimately borrowed from an {{IA}} language of the mountain zone – as Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1950}}: 49) also suggests –, but at least the {{GB}} word is obviously identical to the {{Psht.}} form and most likely borrowed in the other direction. The same can be assumed for the {{Torw.}} form, as the loss of final vowels and *''r-'' > ''ẓ-'' are rather recent changes in {{Torw.}} (cf. ''ẓoz'' 'fast' < {{NP}} ''rōza''). Borrowing from {{Psht.}} is less likely for the {{Pash.}} and {{Shum.}} forms, which may instead reflect something closer to the source of the {{Psht.}} word, though the {{Shum.}} form is possibly a borrowing from {{Pash.}}. An ultimate etymology and/or a link to the Khowar-Kashmiri 'musk deer' word or the Nuristani forms remains, however, unclear, despite an obvious superficial resemblance. Within {{Psht.}}, ''rāmusáy'' ~ ''rambosáy'' can be linked to ''husáy'' ~ ''osáy'' 'deer', whether as an original compound element or as a result of folk-etymological reanalysis.<ref>Note also the semantic development of  borrowed {{Psht.}} ''husay'' 'deer' in {{Gaw.}} ''husey'' 'hare' [{{BKK}}], {{Torw.}} ''husi'' - synonym of ''ẓəmbos'' 'musk deer' [{{TESD}}]</ref> The latter interpretation is favored by the {{Mnj.}} form with final ''z'', which would not be expected in a cognate of {{Psht.}} ''husáy'' ~ ''osáy'', but agrees with the {{IA}} forms.<ref>If the word were an original compound with ''husáy'' ~ ''osáy'', this would leave an element ''rām-'' ~ ''ramb-'', which Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1940}}: 249) proposes to link with {{OIA}} ''rāma-'' 'dark; a kind of antelope'. Such a compound analysis would need to be somehow reconciled with the {{Pash.}}, {{Shum.}} and {{Mnj.}} forms.</ref>

column1: The wide distribution of this word in Indo-Aryan, along with its peculiar ''ṇḍ'', make it likely that it is a loanword. In accordance with the {{OIA}} form, the original root vocalism would appear to be ''i''. Some of the forms are compatible with this, but the vocalism of some of the others points rather to a rounded vowel. It has been suggested that a variant *''puṇḍa-'' could be responsible for some later {{IA}} forms. This form is unattested in {{OIA}}, unless it is the root of ''puṇḍárīka-'' 'lotus flower' (*''puṇḍa'' 'lump' referring to the bulbous blossom?) and/or ''puṇḍ(r)a-'' 'mark, sign, sectarian mark on the forehead' (*''puṇḍa'' 'lump' referring to an originally round shape or a clod of marking paste?). Turner ({{CDIAL}}: T. 8377) also cites {{Pkt.}} ''puṁḍaïa-'' 'lump-shaped, globular', ''poṁḍa-'', ''°aya-'' 'fruit' in support of this variant.

Berger ({{Berger1955}}: 61) has suggested that {{OIA}} ''piṇḍa-'', {{MIA}} ''piṁḍa ~ peṁḍa'' belongs to a group of words from popular registers with uncertain (non-Indo-European?) origins that may have originally (i.e. in a presumable donor language) had short ''ĕ''/''ŏ'' which was substituted in {{OIA}} with ''i''/''u'', but in {{MIA}} more accurately with the ''ĕ''/''ŏ'', which only became available as phonemes at that time. On the other hand, he also proposes a neutralization of the contrast between ''i'' and short ''ĕ'' before a retroflex syllable coda in {{MIA}} (Berger {{Berger1955}}: 62). For this particular word, the assumption of original ''i'' and ''ĕ'' would therefore both be admissible. Either way, the appearance of another variant with ''e'' is not unexpected and need not be due to a ''vr̥ddhi'' formation (with {{MIA}} ''e'' < {{OIA}} ''ai''). It is doubtful whether the Nuristani languages ever developed a contrast between long and short ''e'' in the course of their history. It is therefore possible that {{MIA}} ''ĕ'' was simply mapped onto their phoneme /e/. The Nuristani forms above are grouped according to their possible original root vowels.

The wide distribution of this word in Indo-Aryan, along with its peculiar ṇḍ, make it likely that it is a loanword. In accordance with the OIA form, the original root vocalism would appear to be i. Some of the forms are compatible with this, but the vocalism of some of the others points rather to a rounded vowel. It has been suggested that a variant *puṇḍa- could be responsible for some later IA forms. This form is unattested in OIA, unless it is the root of puṇḍárīka- 'lotus flower' (*puṇḍa 'lump' referring to the bulbous blossom?) and/or puṇḍ(r)a- 'mark, sign, sectarian mark on the forehead' (*puṇḍa 'lump' referring to an originally round shape or a clod of marking paste?). Turner (CDIAL: T. 8377) also cites Pkt. puṁḍaïa- 'lump-shaped, globular', poṁḍa-, °aya- 'fruit' in support of this variant.

Berger (1955: 61) has suggested that OIA piṇḍa-, MIA piṁḍa ~ peṁḍa belongs to a group of words from popular registers with uncertain (non-Indo-European?) origins that may have originally (i.e. in a presumable donor language) had short ĕ/ŏ which was substituted in OIA with i/u, but in MIA more accurately with the ĕ/ŏ, which only became available as phonemes at that time. On the other hand, he also proposes a neutralization of the contrast between i and short ĕ before a retroflex syllable coda in MIA (Berger 1955: 62). For this particular word, the assumption of original i and ĕ would therefore both be admissible. Either way, the appearance of another variant with e is not unexpected and need not be due to a vr̥ddhi formation (with MIA e < OIA ai). It is doubtful whether the Nuristani languages ever developed a contrast between long and short e in the course of their history. It is therefore possible that MIA ĕ was simply mapped onto their phoneme /e/. The Nuristani forms above are grouped according to their possible original root vowels.

Most likely w përë́ in përë́-moč is not to be equated with përë́ 'round' (see below), but is the same word as ne/se purë́ 'complete', which makes more semantic sense.

column1: * '''Proto-Indo-European''' *''u̯erd<sup>h</sup>h<sub>1</sub>o-'' < *''u̯erh<sub>1</sub>-d<sup>h</sup>h<sub>1</sub>o-'', a compound of *''u̯erh<sub>1</sub>-'' 'to say' and ''d<sup>h</sup>eh<sub>1</sub>-'' 'to put, to make' (Hackstein {{Hackstein2002}}: 14)
The different ablaut grades of the various descendant forms have not yet found a definitive explanation (cf. {{NIL}}: 729–730; {{ALEW 2.0}} s.v. ''var̃das'').

Since Morgenstierne ({{Morgenstierne1929}}: 284), these Nuristani forms have been connected with {{PIE}} *''u̯erh<sub>1</sub>-'' 'to say' ({{Gr.}} εἴρω). Based on this, Turner ({{CDIAL}}: T. 11327) reconstructed a Pseudo-{{OIA}} form *''vari-'' 'speech', but this could not account for the ''-r-'', which, in an inherited word, should be dropped in intervocalic position. His proposal of connections with {{OIA}} ''varṇa-'' 'sound, syllable' and ''vā́ṇī-'' 'voice, sound' is doubtful, as the former is more likely a specialized use of ''varṇa-'' 'type, color' and the latter already appears as ''vāṇī-'' in the R̥gveda, which makes it rather implausible to assume a reduction from *''varṇī'' ''vel sim.'', as would be required for a connection with the other words (cf. {{KEWA}} III: 154, 184). It is also difficult to reconcile with the laryngeal which is nowadays reconstructed in {{PIE}} *''u̯erh<sub>1</sub>-''.

On the other hand, a connection with the Indo-European word for 'word', which likely contains the same {{PIE}} root, could account for the ''-r-'' as a reflex of *''-rr-'' < *''-rd-''. The only issue with this explanation is that this etymon does not otherwise appear in Indo-Iranian. Though the {{Kt.}} forms could equally well descend from a form with {{PIIr.}} *''ar'' or *''r̥'' in the first syllable, in {{A.}} the development to *''-rr-'' would not be expected if the root had *''r̥'' (cf. {{A.}} ''židí'' < {{PIIr.}} *''j́<sup>h</sup>r̥dai̯a-''). A reconstruction with *''ar'' is therefore more likely. The final vowel may reflect a suffix *''-iya-'' or *''-ika-''.

The suffixes {{Wakh.}} ''-wor'', {{Kho.}} ''-war'', which appear in language names, have sometimes been connected with the Nuristani forms, but they are most likely unrelated and ultimately borrowed from {{NP}} ''-wār(ī)'' '-like' (as in, e.g., ''šēr-wār'' 'lion-like' [Šāhnāma]) (Steblin-Kamenskij {{Steblin-Kamenskij1999}}: 391). This suffix is attested since the Middle Iranian period (e.g. {{MP}} ''šāh-wār'' 'like a king') (see Durkin-Meisterernst {{Durkin-Meisterernst2014}}: 182) and has been adopted for language names in various cases, e.g. in dialectal Tajik ''vanǰi-vorí'' 'in Vanji' = ""like the Vanjis"" (Steblin-Kamenskij {{Steblin-Kamenskij1999}}: 391) and (as a loanword) in Domari ''ḍōm-wāri'' 'the Domari language', ''tat-wāri'' 'the Arabic language' (Matras {{Matras2012}}: 4). The Nuristani forms, by contrast, are not suffixes, but frequently appear in independent use. They also cannot derive from a form with long *''ā'' in the first syllable.","

[{{DoG}}, {{IIFL III.3}}]. According to von Hinüber ({{vonHinüber2001}}: 202–203) such doublet outcomes of triple consonant clusters would be expected in {{MIA}}.<ref>An alternative way of explaining the developments ⟨riṣ̄⟩/*''iṣin'' < ''r̥ṣṇ'' would be to assume borrowing from {{Skt.}}.</ref> However, in neither of the attested parallel cases the outcome is ''aṇ'' as in the {{NKal.}} word.     [Korn 2005: 210]

• Ossetic bæz- adj. 'thick, dense' [in compounds]
    [IĖSOJa]

Morgenstierne (1929: 249) has compared these forms to OIA bahíṣ- 'outside' and bahir-vāsas- 'outer garment', which would imply that they are inherited cognates derived from a PIIr. *baj́ʰiš-, e.g. as *baj́ʰi-ka- or *baj́ʰi-ra- (though IA has only OIA bāhīká- 'being outside, external', Pa. bāhira- 'external', both with long ā). Semantically this is possible, but it is not clear whether the vowel correspondences in the second syllable allow such a derivation. The available A. evidence is phonologically unreliable, but shows no palatalization of z to ž, which would be expected before *i. The assumption of an original *u in the second syllable would be less problematic.

It may therefore instead be preferable to compare the Nuristani forms to the words for 'thick, dense, coarse' listed above, either as PNur. *baj̈u-ka- or as *baj̈u-ra- (~ OIA bahulá-). Semantically, this would be equally possible, since the garment in question is a thick overcoat.[1]
With either derivation, the development PIIr. *j́ʰ > *j̈ would identify these forms as inherited.

• ↑ A potential comparison with OIA bāhú-, YAv. bāzu- 'arm' (cf. PNur. *bāj̈[u]-), which is perhaps semantically connectable via the notion of 'sleeve', runs into issues with the short vowel in the first syllable. The similarity of Mal. baju 'shirt, jacket' would appear to be accidental, even though this word is usually explained as a loanword from Prs. bāzū 'arm' (Blust et al. 2023), so that a parallel borrowing into Nuristani is theoretically not impossible. However, the derivation of the Mal. from Prs. is quite uncertain, since Prs. bāzū is not attested with the meaning 'shirt'. Additionally, if we were to assume that the Nuristani terms are borrowed from Prs., the short vowel in the first syllable would still be unexpected.

column1: {{NKal.}} ''-nz-'' points to an original cluster, but the identification of this cluster as *''j̈g'' can only be made through external comparison. The {{PIIr.}} cluster *''ds'' merges into an affricate in Iranian and probably Nuristani, but is reduced to ''d'' in {{OIA}} (cf. Halfmann {{Halfmann2025}}: 50).

See Lubotsky ({{Lubotsky2010}}: s.v. ádga-) and {{NIL}} (207–208) for more on {{PIE}}, {{PIIr.}} and {{PCelt.}} reconstructions and for possible further {{IE}} connections. Semantically the Celtic forms show most clearly what the original spectrum of meaning of this word family might have been.

There are many similar, but diverging, {{Prs.}} forms with meanings like 'wart, knot in wood, twig, cluster of grapes' and perhaps not all of them belong here ({{FRZF}} separates ''āzax'' 'wart' from ''azg'' 'twig'), but a detailed study would be required to sort out attestations and dialectal distribution. All attested forms are non-Persid, with ''z'' for {{PIIr.}} *''j́⁽ʰ⁾''; they also all lack the metathesis *''zg'' > ''γz'' seen in {{NP}} ''maγz'' 'brain' < *''mazga-''. They could all go back to one etymon (as assumed by Filippone {{Filippone2011}}: 213), if forms of the type ''ā̆zax'' contain an epenthetic vowel and show final devoicing. The type ''zax'' is explainable via {{NP}} aphaeresis of ''a-''. With these assumptions, {{Khwar.}} ⟨''ʾzx''⟩, {{Psht.}} ''zə́xa'' are most likely Persian loans (resp. ⇐ the variants ''azax'' and ''zax''; secondary addition of the feminine suffix ''-a'' in {{Psht.}} is well-attested).

Herzenberg's ({{Herzenberg2014}}: 42-43) alternative suggestion that {{Prs.}} ''āzax'' may be connected with {{Av.}} ''zaṇga-'' 'ankle', {{MP}} ''zang'' 'ankle, shank', {{Oss.}} ''zæng/zængæ'', {{OIA}} ''jáṅghā-'' 'lower leg, shank' via a meaning of 'something attached', is implausible (thus also Filippone {{Filippone2011}}: 213, fn. 119) and ignores the likely connection of these words to {{PIE}} *''ǵʰengʰ-'' to stride ({{Goth.}} ''gaggan'') ({{EWA}} I: 564, {{LIV2}}: 176).

{{Khwar.}} ''-zγyk'' '-horned' appears only as the second member of compounds referring to types of livestock and does not by itself mean 'horn', as Henning ({{Henning1956}}: 433) implies (cf. {{Khwar.}} ''šw'' 'horn'). It may be a metaphorical use of an adjective *'-twigged' < *''-azg-ika-'' in specialized livestock terminology, and in this way a genuine cognate.","

NKal. -nz- points to an original cluster, but the identification of this cluster as *j̈g can only be made through external comparison. The PIIr. cluster *ds merges into an affricate in Iranian and probably Nuristani, but is reduced to d in OIA (cf. Halfmann 2025: 50).

See Lubotsky (2010: s.v. ádga-) and NIL (207–208) for more on PIE, PIIr. and PCelt. reconstructions and for possible further IE connections. Semantically the Celtic forms show most clearly what the original spectrum of meaning of this word family might have been.

There are many similar, but diverging, Prs. forms with meanings like 'wart, knot in wood, twig, cluster of grapes' and perhaps not all of them belong here (FRZF separates āzax 'wart' from azg 'twig'), but a detailed study would be required to sort out attestations and dialectal distribution. All attested forms are non-Persid, with z for PIIr. *j́⁽ʰ⁾; they also all lack the metathesis *zg > γz seen in NP maγz 'brain' < *mazga-. They could all go back to one etymon (as assumed by Filippone 2011: 213), if forms of the type ā̆zax contain an epenthetic vowel and show final devoicing. The type zax is explainable via NP aphaeresis of a-. With these assumptions, Khwar. ⟨ʾzx⟩, Psht. zə́xa are most likely Persian loans (resp. ⇐ the variants azax and zax; secondary addition of the feminine suffix -a in Psht. is well-attested).

Herzenberg's (2014: 42-43) alternative suggestion that Prs. āzax may be connected with Av. zaṇga- 'ankle', MP zang 'ankle, shank', Oss. zæng/zængæ, OIA jáṅghā- 'lower leg, shank' via a meaning of 'something attached', is implausible (thus also Filippone 2011: 213, fn. 119) and ignores the likely connection of these words to PIE *ǵʰengʰ- to stride (Goth. gaggan) (EWA I: 564, LIV₂: 176).

Khwar. -zγyk '-horned' appears only as the second member of compounds referring to types of livestock and does not by itself mean 'horn', as Henning (1956: 433) implies (cf. Khwar. šw 'horn'). It may be a metaphorical use of an adjective *'-twigged' < *-azg-ika- in specialized livestock terminology, and in this way a genuine cognate.

column1: Turner ({{CDIAL}} T.560) derived the Nuristani words for 'house' from the Vedic form ''amā́'' 'at home' (loc.sg.), but this is phonologically impossible (the final syllable would be lost and the ''l'' in {{Pr.}} remains unexplained). Morgenstierne's ({{Morgenstierne1929}}: 241) derivation < ""*''ā-māta-'' 'built'"" is also phonologically problematic, as the correspondence {{Kt.}} {{ne}} ''u'' ~ {{w}}/{{se}} ''o'' in the second syllable appears to require an original following nasal and the ''l'' in {{Pr.}} again remains unexplained. It is also semantically less straightforward than the derivation from PIIr. *''dmāna-'' 'house' proposed here

There are no necessary phonological reasons why this set of words would have to be considered inherited, but the cognates are universally found throughout the family and the attestations outside of it, in neighboring {{Shum.}} and {{GB}} (both ''āma'' 'house'), are isolated among their relatives. Other {{NIA}} languages have reflexes of {{OIA}} ''gr̥há-'' in the meaning 'house' (cf. also {{NKal.}} ''[[gar]]'' 'house' ⇐ {{IA}}), whereas ''mā́na-'' 'house' is not attested in post-Vedic literary {{IA}} and only has reflexes meaning 'nest'/'spiderweb' in some northwestern {{NIA}} languages (cf. {{CDIAL}} T. 10042 and the {{IA}}-derived doublet {{NKal.}} [[mr̩̆]] 'nest'). The {{Shum.}} and {{GB}} words could be parallel {{IA}} formations of ''ā'' + ''mā́na-'', but most likely they are borrowings from Nuristani, since already the closest relatives {{Gṛan.}} and {{Ning.}} have ''ge'' < ''gr̥há-'' instead and the Nuristani development of PIIr. *''ā'' to a preposition and further into a local prefix (cf. Degener {{Degener1998}}: 139, Halfmann {{Halfmann2024a}}: 227) seems to be unparalleled in {{IA}} (cf. Reinöhl {{Reinöhl2016}}).<ref>Fussman ({{Fussman1972}}: 220) also assumes borrowing from Nuristani, but his reasoning that this must be ""because the 'Kafir' house seemed like the house ''par excellence''"" (""parce que la maison «kafire» semblait la maison par excellence"") is not compelling.</ref> Since the forms are synchronically not treated as containing a local prefix, it is necessary to assume that the local prefix was reanalyzed as a fixed part of the word, as in German ''das Zuhause'' 'the home' < ''zu Hause'' 'at the house'.

The reconstruction of *''d'' at the beginning of the proto-form hinges on the question of whether the ''l'' in {{Pr.}} ''ëmë́l'' reflects a metathesized *''d'' (i.e., *''ā-nmāda-'' < *''ā-dmāna-'') or whether it results from nasal dissimilation in the sequence *''m''V''n''.

Turner (CDIAL T.560) derived the Nuristani words for 'house' from the Vedic form amā́ 'at home' (loc.sg.), but this is phonologically impossible (the final syllable would be lost and the l in Pr. remains unexplained). Morgenstierne's (1929: 241) derivation < ""*ā-māta- 'built'"" is also phonologically problematic, as the correspondence Kt. ne u ~ w/se o in the second syllable appears to require an original following nasal and the l in Pr. again remains unexplained. It is also semantically less straightforward than the derivation from PIIr. *dmāna- 'house' proposed here

There are no necessary phonological reasons why this set of words would have to be considered inherited, but the cognates are universally found throughout the family and the attestations outside of it, in neighboring Shum. and GB (both āma 'house'), are isolated among their relatives. Other NIA languages have reflexes of OIA gr̥há- in the meaning 'house' (cf. also NKal. gar 'house' ⇐ IA), whereas mā́na- 'house' is not attested in post-Vedic literary IA and only has reflexes meaning 'nest'/'spiderweb' in some northwestern NIA languages (cf. CDIAL T. 10042 and the IA-derived doublet NKal. mr̩̆ 'nest'). The Shum. and GB words could be parallel IA formations of ā + mā́na-, but most likely they are borrowings from Nuristani, since already the closest relatives Gṛan. and Ning. have ge < gr̥há- instead and the Nuristani development of PIIr. *ā to a preposition and further into a local prefix (cf. Degener 1998: 139, Halfmann 2024a: 227) seems to be unparalleled in IA (cf. Reinöhl 2016).[4] Since the forms are synchronically not treated as containing a local prefix, it is necessary to assume that the local prefix was reanalyzed as a fixed part of the word, as in German das Zuhause 'the home' < zu Hause 'at the house'.

The reconstruction of *d at the beginning of the proto-form hinges on the question of whether the l in Pr. ëmë́l reflects a metathesized *d (i.e., *ā-nmāda- < *ā-dmāna-) or whether it results from nasal dissimilation in the sequence *mVn.
Pace Strand (1999b), Kt. se samó 'dance' etc. does not belong here.

Many regional {{NIA}} languages have forms resembling those of the Nuristani languages, but the Nuristani forms differ from those in most surrounding {{IA}} languages in reflecting a nasal second syllable. In neighboring {{IA}} languages this is only found in {{GB}} and {{Shum.}},<ref>{{S.}} ""''ac̣hē̃''"" is not confirmed by Buddruss ({{Buddruss1967}}: 80) who noted ''ẽc̣hī́'', which agrees with the audio recording of Liljegren et al. ({{Liljegren2021}})</ref> but these languages appear to reflect an original *''ī̆'' in the second syllable, whereas the vowel correspondence in the second syllable of the Nuristani forms excludes the reconstruction of an original *''ī̆''.

Following the argumentation of Halfmann ({{Halfmann2025}}: 66–75), the ''č'' in the Nuristani forms cannot be considered a regular inherited outcome of {{PIE}} *''kʷs'' that would correspond to {{OIA}} *''kṣ''. The Nuristani forms other than {{Tr.}} could in theory reflect an original palatal affricate from a formation like {{PIE}} *''h₃ekʷ-en-'' (cf. {{NIL}}: 371), but such a formation is otherwise not directly attested within Indo-Iranian.

Several of the surrounding {{IA}} languages have palatal affricates (or dental affricates developed out of palatals) reflecting {{OIA}} ''kṣ'' in this word. These result in some cases from mergers of earlier ''c̣'' and ''č'' in ''č'' (e.g. in Southeastern {{Pash.}}), in other cases from secondary palatalizations of the retroflex affricate arising from {{OIA}} ''kṣ'' by a following ''i'' (cf. Halfmann {{Halfmann2025}}: 66–69). The stem of the Nuristani forms can therefore be considered a loanword from {{IA}}. The contrastive retroflex in the {{Tr.}} form, still doubted by Halfmann ({{Halfmann2025}}: 68, fn. 84), has now been confirmed in an interview with a native speaker and strongly indicates borrowing from {{IA}}. Variation between a retroflex and a palatal reflex of {{OIA}} ''kṣ'' occurs even within the closely related Kunar group, where {{GB}} and {{Shum.}} have ''ċ'' < *''č'', but {{Ning.}} and {{Gṛan.}} have ''c̣''. This could point to a parallel persistence of two variants, possibly arising from paradigmatic variation (inflectional forms with and without following *''i''), until rather recent times. It is possible that both variants were at one point borrowed into all Nuristani languages, but it is also possible that the retroflex variant only ever entered {{Tr.}}.

The suffix of the Nuristani forms remains to be explained. Halfmann ({{Halfmann2025}}: 68, fn. 84) proposes that an inherited ending *''-āni'' equivalent to Vedic {{OIA}} nom./acc. pl. ''-ā́ṇi'' could have been added to the borrowed stem, but the exact process of how this could have happened is difficult to motivate. An alternative explanation would be that the Vedic plural ending ''-ā́ṇi'' persisted in earlier {{IA}} languages of the region and thence entered into Nuristani as part of a paradigm nom.sg. *''acchi'', nom./acc. pl. *''ac̣c̣hāṇi'' ~ *''acchāni''. However, in other regions this ending seems to have already been lost by the {{MIA}} period.

Functionally, the development is similar to that of ''-pāla-(ka-)'' 'guardian' as a final member of compounds, which became a versatile nominal suffix over the course of {{IA}} history, referring to people associated with the base of derivation (Négyesi {{Négyesi2005}}) and was also borrowed into Nuristani (see [[pālaga]]). A comparable semantic development (though with much more limited productivity) happened with the English word/suffix ''(-)monger'', which was extended from contexts like ''fish-monger'' to formations like ''war-monger''.<ref>While such a development is plausible in general, it is not necessarily the case that all functions of all the attested suffixes are etymologically derived from {{MIA}} ''vāniya''. Some of them could be due to secondary homonymy with other etyma.</ref>

Judging from the overlapping semantic spectrum of the comparable suffixes in {{GB}} and {{Pash.}},<ref>The functional spectrum of the {{Pash.}} suffix is not well-documented enough for definite conclusions about its etymology.</ref> it is possible that the functional reanalysis was already completed in the {{IA}} source language when the element entered Nuristani.

The origin of the {{Kt.}} feminine form is not fully clear. Perhaps it is identical with the feminine form of [[vo]]/[[vay]] 'having', secondarily associated with a form that was originally only masculine.

The derivation of {{Pr.}} ''wuni'' from {{PIIr.}} *''-u̯ant-'' 'having' proposed by Buddruss & Degener ({{Buddruss & Degener2015}}: 844) is phonologically problematic. It seems more likely that the suffix is borrowed from {{Kt.}}, as proposed here, with specialization of its function to that of marking ownership and some functional convergence with the proprietives of the other Nuristani languages ({{Kt.}} [[vo]]/[[vay]], {{NKal.}} [[oda]]/[[odi]]).
See also {{MIA}} [[*vāṇijja]] from the same root.

• Young Avestan saii- v. itr. 'to lie down, to go to sleep'
• °saiiana- n. 'resting place, home' [in dužakō.saiiana- adj. 'where the hedgehog has his resting place/home']
An inherited word due to PIIr. *ć > PNur. *ċ.

Turner derives these words from a reconstructed pseudo-OIA form *ut-śiras- (i.e., PIIr. *ud + *ćr̥Has-), citing the parallel of IA forms like OIA ucchīrṣaka- n. n. 'that which raises the head, pillow', Pkt. ussīsa- n. n. 'pillow', but the Nuristani words require a nasal rather than a rhotic in the ancestral form and do not have much in common with the reflexes of PIIr. *ćr̥Has-.

The fact that the Kt. forms have a segmental nasal instead of vowel nasalization is explainable as an analogical generalization of the original non-direct stem ending in *-n̆- (cf. Halfmann 2024a: 134–136).

The Kt. ne form aċén̆ may derive from a different formation *ā-ċayana- with PIIr. *ā instead of *u̯i (cf. OIA ā-śay- 'to lie or rest on', MP āsāy- 'to rest'), though in view of the agreement of all other dialects and languages it is worth considering whether it could instead be explained as an analogical creation (extracted from a prefixed locative?).
